t.ubsu nur@50.6,93.1:
Ubsu-Nur, or Uvs Nuur, is a lake in a land of extremes. It lies in a closed basin on the border between Mongolia and the Russian republic of Tuva, in the middle of Central Asia, where there is no outlet to the sea, so the water simply evaporates, leaving it too salty to drink. It is the largest lake in Mongolia by area, shallow, with wide marshes and reed beds, and it sits between the Altai mountains to the west and the Sayan range to the north. The Tes river, which feeds the lake, gives its name to a part of the basin, and the whole area was listed by UNESCO in 2003 as the Uvs Nuur Basin.

What makes it special is the sheer variety packed into a small space. Within a few hours' travel you pass from desert to steppe, to mountain forest, to tundra and glaciers, and the basin is a stopping point for migrating birds, including swans, cranes and pelicans, as well as a refuge for snow leopards, argali sheep and ibex in the surrounding mountains. The winters are famously harsh, with temperatures falling below minus forty degrees, and summers can be hot, so the lake freezes solid for months.

Travelling here is an expedition. The nearest large town on the Mongolian side is Ulaangom, with fuel and basic services, but distances are huge and fuel stations are far apart outside towns. The road network consists of some paved stretches and a lot of tracks, which turn to mud after rain and drifts in winter. Carry spare fuel, food and water, a repair kit and a satellite messenger, and avoid travelling alone.

Mongolian herders live here in felt tents, called gers, with flocks of sheep, goats, horses and camels, and they will offer salty milk tea and dried curd to a visitor. Accept politely. The best season is June to September, when the steppe is green, with mosquitoes near the marshes. Cold arrives early, and in September the first snow can fall on the high ground. The sky at night, with no light for hundreds of kilometres, is the reason to stay.
t.oroku shinaa@50.6,94.0:
The Uvs Nuur Basin is one of those places on the map that looks like a mistake. A huge salt lake, a ring of mountains, a dry steppe, a patch of desert and a snowfield, all within a few hours of each other. The basin straddles the border between Mongolia and Russia, and the Russian part lies in Tuva, a republic of throat singers, shamans and horse herders in the heart of Siberia. Oroku-Shinaa, in the northern part, is one of the clusters protected as part of the UNESCO site listed in 2003.

The point of the basin is variety. Within a modest distance you pass from alpine tundra at the top of the Tannu-Ola mountains down through larch forest, steppe and semi-desert to the shores of Uvs Nuur, which is a saline lake with a fringe of reedbeds. It is a refuge for snow leopards and argali sheep in the high country, for birds on the lake, and for the animals of the steppe. Tuva is also an old centre of nomadic culture, and the burial mounds and standing stones of the Scythian era are scattered across the landscape.

Riding in Tuva means a mix of asphalt on the main route from Kyzyl, the capital, and dirt tracks that turn dusty in summer and boggy after rain. The weather is continental, with hot short summers and savage winters. July and August are warm, although a thunderstorm can arrive quickly on the open plain.

Carry fuel and water, check your route for border zone restrictions, since this is near an international frontier, and expect curiosity from herders you meet. Tuvans are known for khoomei, a throat-singing style that produces two notes at once, and if you hear it live you will not forget it. The best light is early or late, when the mountains turn blue and the steppe goes gold.
t.anchorage@61.2,-149.9:
Anchorage lies where Cook Inlet meets the Chugach mountains, a city of about three hundred thousand people that holds nearly half of Alaska's population and yet ends abruptly at the edge of the forest. Moose wander through the suburbs, and on a clear day, the snowy peaks of the Alaska Range, including Denali far to the north, float on the horizon. The city grew from a railway construction camp in 1915, and was badly damaged by the Good Friday earthquake in 1964, among the most powerful ever recorded.

The Seward Highway begins here and is one of the most scenic roads in North America. It runs south along Turnagain Arm, a long, narrow inlet with some of the highest tidal ranges in the United States. At certain times, a bore tide, a wave a metre or so high, rolls up the inlet, and watchers line the roadside to see it. Beluga Point, as the name suggests, is a good place to spot white whales feeding in summer, and Dall sheep graze on the cliffs above the road.

Riding is easy and beautiful. The road is well paved, with sweeping views, though speed limits are enforced, and traffic gets heavy on summer weekends, with campers, trucks and fishermen headed for the Kenai Peninsula. Weather can change quickly, with rain and wind coming off the inlet, and mornings can be cool even in July. Long daylight in midsummer, with the sun barely setting, means plenty of time for riding, and wildlife such as moose on the road is a serious hazard at dawn and dusk. Autumn brings gold birch and cottonwood, and ice and snow arrive in October.

Anchorage has everything: fuel stations, motorcycle shops, supermarkets and a wide range of lodging. South of the city, fuel is available at Girdwood and Portage, though services are thin along the inlet, so fill up before leaving. The Alaska Railway Museum, Potter Marsh bird sanctuary and Alyeska Resort are all worth a stop. Try smoked salmon or reindeer sausage on the way, and carry rain gear and bear spray if you plan to hike.
t.moose pass@60.5,-149.4:
Moose Pass is a small cluster of cabins, a general store and a roadhouse beside a turquoise lake, and the speed limit through it is low for good reason. The village lies on the Kenai Peninsula in south-central Alaska, about forty kilometres north of Seward on the Seward Highway, and perhaps two hundred people live here. Trail Lake, in front of the village, is fed by glacial meltwater, and the water has the milky blue-green colour of ground rock, which makes the whole valley glow. Mountains still holding patches of snow rise on both sides, and spruce forest covers the lower slopes.

The place has a friendly, local character. Every June, around the summer solstice, the village holds a festival with a parade, a barbecue and a small bake sale, and the community hall hosts events through the year. The Alaska Railroad runs through, and the train from Anchorage to Seward, one of the great scenic rail journeys, passes the village. The surrounding area is rich in wildlife, with moose wandering through the village, bald eagles and, in summer, salmon running in the streams. Brown and black bears are present, so store food carefully, and keep a distance from any animal.

The Seward Highway, which links Anchorage and Seward, is a designated All-American Road and one of the most beautiful in the country. South of Moose Pass the road follows the shore of Kenai Lake and then descends to Resurrection Bay at Seward. To the north it climbs through the Chugach Mountains, passing Summit Lake and the pass, then drops toward Turnagain Arm. The surface is good, but the road is busy in summer with RVs and fishing traffic, and passing zones are limited, so take it patiently. Weather can change quickly, with rain, fog and even snow at the higher points.

Fuel and food are limited in Moose Pass itself, and the nearest larger service centres are at Seward or Cooper Landing, so top up before you arrive. The roadhouse serves hearty meals, and the bakery is popular. In summer the days stretch to nearly twenty hours of light, and the late evening glow on the lake is magical.
t.kyzyl@51.7,94.4:
Asia has a centre, according to Kyzyl, and the city has put up an obelisk to prove it. It stands on the bank of the Yenisei at the point where the Bii-Khem and Kaa-Khem rivers meet to form the Ulug-Khem, the upper Yenisei, and a stone globe and inscription declare the spot to be the Centre of Asia. Whether the claim is serious or not, the place is a fine one, with wide blue water and mountains on the horizon, in the middle of the Republic of Tuva.

Tuva has a strange modern history. It was an independent state, Tannu Tuva, from 1921 until 1944, when it was absorbed by the Soviet Union, and its stamps, triangular and diamond-shaped, were famous with collectors, among them the physicist Richard Feynman, who tried for years to visit. The Tuvans are traditionally nomadic herders, followers of Tibetan Buddhism mixed with older shamanic beliefs, and they are famous for throat singing, khoomei, in which one singer produces two or more notes at once. The sound, low and whistling, seems to come from the steppe itself.

The Yenisei Highway from Abakan to Kyzyl is one of the great road journeys of Siberia. It climbs through the Sayan Mountains, passing high passes, forested slopes and the huge Sayano-Shushenskaya reservoir, and then descends into the dry, open basin of Tuva, with yurts and herds of horses and sheep. The road is mostly asphalt, though patched, and in places narrow and winding, with trucks and sudden changes of weather. Snow can fall even in summer on the high passes. The road toward Ak-Dovurak runs west through bare hills and steppe, with long empty stretches.

Kyzyl has more than a hundred thousand people, so fuel, food and hotels are easy to find, with Kaa-Khem and Sukpak nearby offering more. Local food includes mutton, dumplings and salty milk tea. Summers are short and hot, winters cold and dry. Foreign riders should check current conditions and rules before planning travel in this region.
t.papeete@-17.6,-149.6:
Papeete is not the Tahiti of the posters, and that is rather its charm. It is a busy, slightly shabby, humid Pacific capital of some twenty-six thousand people, with another few hundred thousand in the sprawl around it on the north-west coast of the island, and it works hard at being a normal French town. Scooters weave through the traffic, bakeries sell baguettes at dawn, and the harbour is full of ferries heading for Moorea, which lies like a jagged green wall on the horizon.

The market is the heart of it. The Marché de Papeete, a large covered hall in the centre, sells flowers, fruit, vanilla, monoi oil, pearls and woven goods, and on Sunday mornings it opens before dawn and fills with people. At night the waterfront comes alive with the roulottes, food trucks that serve grilled fish, steak frites, chow mein and crepes at plastic tables. It is cheap, friendly and the best dinner in town. Tahitian pearls are the local luxury, and the shops along the front sell them at every price.

A short way east, at Pointe Vénus, the captain James Cook observed the transit of Venus in 1769, and the mutineers of the Bounty first landed here a couple of decades later. The black sand beach and the white lighthouse are worth a stop. Paul Gauguin lived on the island and the French connection is everywhere, in the language, the cuisine and the Paris-style prices, which are high.

For riding, the coastal road around Tahiti Nui is a good outing of about a hundred and fifteen kilometres, with the sea on one side and steep green hills on the other. Traffic in and around Papeete is dreadful at rush hour, so leave early. Beyond the city the road quietens, with waterfalls, black sand beaches and little villages, and the bends are easy but often wet. Rain showers are frequent, particularly from November to April, and the surface can be slick.

Fuel and services are plentiful around Papeete, and you should fill up before leaving, since stations thin out away from the capital. Eat at the roulottes at least once, wear a light waterproof, and enjoy the heat.

The cooler dry season, roughly May to October, is best for riding.
t.seward@60.1,-149.4:
Alaska's Seward Highway earns its reputation from beginning to end, and Seward is where it runs out of road. The town sits at the head of Resurrection Bay, a fjord on the Kenai Peninsula ringed by steep, snow-streaked mountains, and it has a working harbour full of fishing boats, tour vessels and the occasional cruise ship. It was founded in 1903 as the ocean terminus for a railroad to the interior, and it is also mile zero of the Iditarod Trail, the dog-sledding route to Nome. The 1964 Good Friday earthquake, the most powerful ever recorded in North America, destroyed much of the waterfront here, and the town has rebuilt itself since.

The road in is the highlight. From Anchorage, the highway follows Turnagain Arm, a long inlet with huge tides, where a tidal bore sometimes rolls up the channel and belugas swim close to shore. Past Portage, it climbs through spruce forest, skirts glacial lakes, crosses Turnagain Pass at 988 feet, and runs through Moose Pass before dropping to the bay. About 127 miles in total, it is a mostly two-lane road with passing zones, scenic pull-offs and heavy summer traffic, including motorhomes, so patience is essential. Dress for cold and wet, since fog and rain are common, and watch for moose near the road.

Seward has a small downtown with restaurants, a waterfront trail and the Alaska SeaLife Center, which cares for stranded marine animals. Boats leave for the Kenai Fjords National Park, where tidewater glaciers calve into the sea and humpback whales, sea otters and puffins can be seen. Exit Glacier, reached by a short road from town, is one of the easiest places in Alaska to walk up to the ice. On the Fourth of July, runners race up and down Mount Marathon, a steep climb above the town, which is the town's great event.

Fuel and food are available in Seward, which has about 2,800 residents. The best season runs from mid-May to mid-September, when days are very long and the roads are clear.
t.eklutna@61.5,-149.4:
Eklutna is a place where the old and the new Alaska sit side by side. A few miles north of Anchorage, where the Glenn Highway runs along the shore of Knik Arm with the Chugach Mountains rearing up on the east side, a small Dena'ina Athabascan village, the oldest continuously inhabited site in the Anchorage area, keeps its traditions in the shadow of a motorway. The village is home to a small Russian Orthodox church, a log building dedicated to Saint Nicholas, one of the oldest buildings in the region, and a graveyard with a unique feature: colourful little wooden spirit houses, painted and decorated, stand over the graves, a blend of Dena'ina and Orthodox traditions. The effect is quiet and moving.

Not far away, Eklutna Lake is a long, narrow glacial lake in Chugach State Park, wedged between steep mountains and fed by glaciers, with water of a milky turquoise. It is the main source of drinking water for Anchorage, and the road in follows the lake shore for miles. The area is excellent for hiking, cycling, and paddling, and on a clear day the scenery is magnificent. Wasilla and Knik-Fairview lie a short way north, and are the biggest towns around.

The Glenn Highway is a fast, well-built road, running through a valley with views of mountains and water, and it is the main route from Anchorage to the Matanuska Valley and beyond. Traffic is heavy at commuting hours, but eases as you head north. In summer the days are long, with light until nearly midnight, and the roads are dry, though frost heaves and patches of gravel can appear. Wildlife is plentiful, and moose are a real hazard on the road, particularly at dusk and dawn, and in winter. Keep a sharp lookout.

Fuel is available at Eagle River and Wasilla, and at service stations along the highway, but you should not count on them in the evenings. Take water, snacks and a warm layer, since the weather in the mountains can change rapidly. Mosquitoes are fierce in June and July, and bear spray is a sensible precaution on any trail. The long evening light on the water, the silence and the smell of spruce make this one of the best places to stop in southern Alaska.
t.matanuska glacier@61.8,-147.8:
The Matanuska Glacier is a river of ice twenty-seven miles long and about four miles wide at its end, one of the biggest glaciers you can drive to in the United States. It spills out of the Chugach Mountains in a great grey-white tongue, ribbed with crevasses and streaked with dirt, and its meltwater runs off in the Matanuska River, a braided stream of milky grey water that wanders across a wide gravel bed. You can see the glacier from the highway, at a state viewpoint near mile 101 of the Glenn Highway, where the whole ice mass lies spread out below like a frozen sea. If you want to walk on the ice, you must cross private land, and a fee is charged.

The Glenn Highway between Palmer and Glennallen is a fine road, running through a landscape of rock, spruce and river, with mountains on both sides. It climbs through the Matanuska Valley, past farms where huge cabbages are grown in the long summer days of the far north, then enters wilder country, with the Chugach on the south side and the Talkeetna Mountains on the north. The road is wide and well surfaced, with long curves and good views, but frost heaves, patched tarmac and sudden weather changes can catch the unwary. Rain and wind are common, and snow is possible in any month at the higher points.

The weather around the glacier is cool and often windy, as cold air pours off the ice, and even in July you may want a jacket. Mosquitoes are plentiful in the valley, and the glacier itself is a quiet, ancient place, with the ice creaking and the streams running in blue channels. The sound of meltwater under the surface is a reminder of how alive the glacier is.

Fuel is available in Palmer, about fifty miles back, and at one or two lodges and stations along the road, but they are few and far between, so fill up before you go. Food is limited to a few roadside lodges serving burgers and coffee, and it is worth carrying snacks and water. Keep an eye out for moose and sheep, and for Dall sheep on the cliffs near Sheep Mountain, where they graze in summer. In the long evenings, the glacier takes on a pink glow, and the light lasts until late.
t.abakan@53.7,91.4:
Abakan is the capital of Khakassia and the biggest city for a long way in any direction, with about 167,000 people on the flat bottom of the Minusinsk Basin, where the Abakan River meets the Yenisei. For a rider it is the great resupply point. Everything you might want after days of empty road is here: fuel on every corner, supermarkets, repair shops, hotels, cafes serving everything from Khakass dumplings to Uzbek plov, and traffic lights that you will be oddly glad to see. Nothing else on the Yenisei Highway towards Kyzyl is as well stocked.

The basin around it has an unexpectedly deep past. Dry hills dotted with burial mounds and standing stones from the Bronze Age onwards lie within an hour or two of the city, and the Khakass, a Turkic people, still live here alongside Russians who arrived in the eighteenth and nineteenth centuries. The local museum is known for its collection of carved stone figures from the steppe, and if you have an hour at the end of the day, it is the best way to understand why this flat land feels so occupied by the dead.

The riding changes character as you leave town. North of the city the highway runs fast and dry across the steppe, but heading south and west toward Tuva it begins to rise, with the Western Sayan filling the horizon and the road following the Yenisei towards the great reservoir behind the Sayano-Shushenskaya dam. The asphalt is generally good, gradients are modest at first, and the bends get longer and more fun as the hills close in. Summer is hot, and by midday the pavement shimmers, so start early. Winter is bitter, and snow can close higher sections.

Fill the tank here even if it is still half full. Beyond Abakan the towns thin out, and a closed station or a queue can spoil an afternoon. Pick up water, snacks and a spare layer, because the weather in the mountains can differ completely from what you left in the basin. And leave a little time to wander the riverfront in the evening, when the heat softens and the long light falls across the bridges and the steppe beyond.
t.ergaki@52.8,93.3:
Ergaki is the name of a ridge, a park and a whole mood, and it belongs to the Western Sayan, the great band of mountains that separates the Minusinsk Basin from Tuva. The jagged skyline here is famous across Siberia for the outline called the Sleeping Sayan, a long crest that, from the right angle, resembles a reclining giant lying on his back. Peaks rise above two thousand metres, there are alpine lakes with cold, clear water, and the forest below is a dark carpet of cedar and fir.

The nearest village, Tanzybey, is about forty kilometres away, and it is small. There is no big supermarket or reliable petrol pump up here, so fill the tank and the water bottle in Abakan or in a larger town on the highway before turning off. The approach road leaves the Yenisei Highway and climbs into the mountains on a surface that changes from asphalt to gravel and finally to rough track, with stream crossings and loose stones, so it suits a smaller bike and a rider who likes a bit of mud. After rain the track can turn slick, and in spring melt it can be impassable. Do not be too proud to turn round.

The reward is the scenery. The air is cooler and smells of resin and wet stone, the light at dawn is gold on the ridge, and in late summer the meadows below the cliffs are full of flowers. The lakes with names like Raduzhnoye and Svetloye sit in glacial hollows, and a short walk from the end of the track often brings you to one. Weather moves fast, with cold mornings and afternoon storms, so waterproofs and warm layers should travel with you, even in July.

The area is a nature park, so the usual rules apply: stay on the track, take your rubbish home, and ask locally about any entry fee or restrictions. Hikers and climbers come here from all over the region, and in high season you will meet tents and campfires in the lower valleys. If you can, come on a weekday in early September, when the crowds have thinned and the larch is starting to turn, and the Sleeping Sayan looks down on you in perfect quiet.
t.ak dovurak@51.2,90.6:
Ak-Dovurak means white clay in Tuvan, and the name comes from the pale deposits that gave the town its reason to exist. It grew in the 1950s around an asbestos mine in the western part of the Tuva Republic, and for decades the extraction and processing plant shaped everything about the place. Today around twelve thousand people live in a mix of Soviet blocks and low wooden houses spread across a dry valley, with the little town of Kyzyl-Mazhalyk just over four kilometres away.

For a rider it is a good place to take stock. After a long climb out of the Yenisei basin and across the dry Tuvan uplands, the town offers fuel, shops, simple cafes and a bed for the night, which counts for a lot in a region where settlements can be a day apart. Larger Teeli is thirty kilometres or so away, but beyond that, supplies thin out, so fill up here before heading further. Nothing about the town is polished, but the people are direct and often curious about travellers on motorcycles.

The landscape around it is classic Tuva: treeless hills the colour of toast, long valleys of steppe, and the ridge of the Tannu-Ola range somewhere off to the south. The road is mostly asphalt but badly broken in places, with frost heave and potholes that you want to see before you hit them. Summer is dry and hot, and the sky is a deep, clean blue, while winter is fierce and the wind can cut across the open ground. Late spring and early autumn are the best seasons, with light that makes the hills glow.

Tuva has its own culture, distinct from the rest of Russia. The Tuvans are Turkic-speaking herders with a Buddhist and shamanic tradition, and the republic only joined the Soviet Union in 1944, having been independent for some years before. The country is famous for throat-singing, a technique in which a single singer produces two or more notes at once, and you may hear it on a car radio or at a market. Buy some local bread, drink the salty milk tea if you are offered it, and let the day settle.
t.handagayty@50.7,92.1:
Khandagayty lies in western Tuva, a small town of about three thousand people in country that feels like the end of the Russian map. The border with Mongolia is close, and the town functions as a frontier settlement, with the border crossing nearby shaping everything from the roads to the businesses. Mountains edge the horizon in every direction, bare and brown in summer, white from autumn, with narrow river valleys threading between them.

Reaching it from Kyzyl is a long day's ride across the broad Tuvan basin and into higher, wilder land. The road is a mix of reasonably good asphalt and rougher sections where the surface has broken up, and there is little traffic beyond trucks heading for the border. Corners are rare and gentle, but the weather is the real hazard: wind can build quickly across open ground, and summer storms bring sudden cold rain. Start early, check the sky, and carry layers even in July. Cold nights and bright days are the rule at this altitude.

Fuel and food are limited but available, and you should fill up in the last larger town before you come rather than rely on the pumps at the end. Chadan and other Tuvan centres lie along the way, and they are the places to buy supplies. In Khandagayty itself there are shops for the basics and a few simple cafes, and the locals are used to travellers and to long-distance truckers who have been waiting for border formalities. Because of the frontier, carry your passport and keep your itinerary clear if you are asked.

The wider region is rich in traces of the past. Western Tuva is dotted with ancient burial mounds, stone figures and rock carvings from peoples who crossed these steppes long before borders existed, and the area is part of the cultural landscape that links Siberia, Mongolia and Central Asia. Wild camping is possible but demands care, as nights are cold and the nearest help may be hours away. Watch the sky at dusk, when the high ridges glow pink and the wind finally drops, and you will feel how far you have come from the traffic lights of Krasnoyarsk.
t.jamaalyg@50.3,94.8:
Tuva sits at the geographic heart of Asia, a Russian republic wedged between Siberia and Mongolia, and its south-west corner is a country of salt lakes, steppe and drifting sand. The village of Erzin lies near the Mongolian border in the Ubsunur hollow, a vast basin ringed by mountains, and the dunes of Tsugeer Els are part of a shared World Heritage site with Mongolia, listed in 2003. Jamaalyg is a spot on this wide plain, in the emptiest part of a thinly populated republic.

The Ubsunur basin is a place of extremes. Temperatures swing from forty below in winter to above thirty in summer, with winds that rearrange the dunes and a dry climate that supports a specialised flora and fauna. Saker falcons, steppe eagles and Pallas's cats live in the steppe, and the region is a crossing point for migrating birds. Tuvan herders move their sheep, goats, horses and yaks between pastures in a pattern that has changed little for centuries, living in felt tents, yurts, in summer. Tuva is also the home of khoomei, the throat singing that produces two notes at once, and the music seems to belong to this landscape of wind and space.

For a rider, this is serious country. Tuva has few paved roads, the main ones being the Yenisei highway, which connects Kyzyl, the capital, to the north and to Mongolia, and the roads near the border are rough, and often unmade. The border area is a restricted zone, and foreigners need permits to travel in it, which should be arranged well in advance. Summer is the only comfortable season, though even then nights can be cold.

Erzin is a small village, and fuel and supplies are limited, with the nearest large town being Kyzyl, a long way to the north. Carry spare fuel, food, water and tools, tell someone where you are going, and expect no phone signal. In Kyzyl, a monument marks the centre of Asia, a favourite place for photographs, and the national museum has a good collection of Scythian gold from the nearby Valley of the Kings, which is worth seeing.
t.tes river@50.5,93.5:
Where the Tes river comes down from the Mongolian highlands to the Uvs basin, in the far north-west of the country, the land is open, stony and almost without trees. It flows toward Uvs Nuur, the largest lake in Mongolia, a shallow body of salt water that has no outlet, shared with the Russian republic of Tuva, and the whole basin is a UNESCO site, listed in 2003 as one of the best preserved steppe ecosystems in Central Asia. The delta of the river is a wetland where reeds, marsh and pools attract migrating birds, including swans, pelicans, cranes and many ducks.

The basin is a place of contrasts, with snowy mountains, deserts, steppe, tundra and wetland within a few hours of each other, and its animals include snow leopards, ibex, argali sheep and, in the sands, jerboas and gerbils. The Uvs depression is one of the coldest places in Mongolia in winter, with temperatures that fall to forty below, and in summer it can be hot enough to make the salt flats shimmer.

The people are herders of the Dörvöd and other western Mongol groups, who live in felt gers and move their sheep, goats, horses and camels with the seasons. Visitors are usually welcomed with salted milk tea and dried curds, and it is polite to accept, and equally polite to ask before taking photographs. The ancient history includes Scythian burial mounds, stone figures and rock art that stretch back thousands of years, all scattered through the landscape.

The riding here is real adventure. Outside the main road toward Ulaangom, the provincial capital, there is no pavement to speak of, only tracks on gravel and sand, and rivers must be forded. A good map and GPS, enough fuel, spare tubes and food are essential, and it makes sense to travel with a partner, since mobile coverage is patchy. The best time is June to September, when the days are long and warm; the nights can still be cold, and sudden storms are common. Mosquitoes in the delta can be fierce in midsummer.

No town stands close to this point, so take fuel from Ulaangom before setting out and carry reserve. In the evening, as the light falls low across the salt lake, the whole country goes quiet, and the line of the horizon seems very far away. It is a place for those who like silence.
t.aryskannyg@50.7,94.7:
Tuva sits in the heart of Asia, in a basin enclosed by the Sayan and Tannu-Ola ranges, and its geographical centre was once marked by a monument at Kyzyl, where the Yenisei begins its long journey north. This point lies in the western half of the republic, near Samagaltay, in country of steppe, river terraces and dry hills. Tuva is known for throat singing, for felt yurts and horses, and for a landscape strewn with the stone mounds and carved slabs of people who herded here thousands of years ago. The Scythian-era burial mound at Arzhan, in the east of the republic, held gold animal figures that rank among the glories of ancient steppe art.

Aryskannyg and the Jamaalyg area belong to that archaeological backdrop, with Bronze Age and early nomad monuments spread across the terraces. Stone circles, standing slabs and low cairns lie in the grass, often unfenced, and old women and children may be grazing sheep or goats beside them. In June the steppe is a mass of flowers, and by September it has turned the colour of straw.

Riding in Tuva is remote and satisfying. The main roads are mostly paved but rough, with frost heaves, potholes and long gaps without services, and side tracks are gravel or earth. The weather has big swings, with scorching summer days and freezing nights, and winter is extreme, falling to minus forty. June to early September is the practical season. Wind is persistent, and rivers can run high after heavy rain in the mountains.

Samagaltay, about twenty kilometres away, is a small town with a few shops, cafés and a fuel station, but it is the sort of place where supplies run out, so carry spare fuel and fill up whenever you pass a pump. Kyzyl, the capital, is the better place for lodging and repairs. Food tends to be mutton, dumplings, dairy and strong tea with milk and salt. Russian border zone rules apply near Mongolia, and foreign visitors may need a permit for some districts, so check before you plan a route.
t.tsagan shuvuut@50.3,91.2:
Tsagan Shuvuut means roughly white mountain-range in Mongolian, and the name fits. High in the far north-west, near the meeting point of Tuva and Mongolia, the range rises into snow and rock, and the slopes are dark with larch and cedar taiga lower down. This is the Altai-Sayan country, where Siberian forest meets Central Asian steppe, and it feels like both at once.

The nearby Mongun-Taiga massif is the high point of the area, a glaciated mountain over three thousand metres, and the landscape here is wild: alpine meadows with marmots, streams running cold and clear, and the odd herder's camp. Snow leopard and argali sheep live in these ranges, though you are far more likely to see eagles, vultures and ground squirrels than anything shy. The light is hard and bright, and the air thin enough to make walking uphill feel serious.

Riding in this corner is a different sport from touring in Europe. The roads, where they exist, are tracks of dirt and stone, crossed by streams and sometimes washed out. Weather arrives fast, and a clear morning can turn into a hailstorm by two. Plan the whole loop with spare fuel on board, take food, and ride with someone if you can. A solo breakdown here is a real problem, not an anecdote.

What you get in return is silence and scale. You can stop on a ridge, turn off the engine, and hear wind, a distant sheep bell and nothing else. Early July to early September is the sensible window, with the snow gone from the lower passes and mosquitoes at a tolerable level. In the other months, expect snow and frozen ground. If you meet a herder, a bit of patience and a smile go a long way, and tea will often follow.
t.uvs nuur basin@50.3,92.7:
Uvs Nuur is a lake in a basin, and the basin matters more than the lake. The depression lies astride the border between Mongolia and the Russian republic of Tuva, ringed by mountains on three sides, and it is the northern end of the Central Asian steppe and the southern edge of the Siberian taiga. Within a few hours of each other you can find desert dunes, steppe, mountain tundra, glaciers, forest and salt marsh. UNESCO listed it in 2003 as a transboundary site, and Russia and Mongolia manage their sides separately.

The lake itself is the largest in Mongolia by area, but shallow and very salty, with water too saline to drink and fish that are mostly limited to the river mouths. Its shores and the mouths of the rivers, notably the Tes, are important for migrating waterbirds and for breeding species like swans, cranes and cormorants. In the surrounding steppe, you can see gazelles, and farther up, ibex, argali and the occasional snow leopard.

The riding is gravel and dirt, often flat and fast, sometimes with deep sand or soft salt crust near the shore. A flat horizon makes distances deceptive, and a good-looking track can end in a washed-out ditch. Weather moves fast: summer days are warm, nights can be cold, and the wind is a daily companion. Winter here is severe, with temperatures dropping far below freezing, so late May to September is the realistic window.

Plan fuel carefully. The nearest services may be far from this point, depending on which side of the border you approach from, and mobile coverage is patchy. Carry extra fuel, water, spares, and a way to call for help. Border zones are sensitive, and permits and passports may be checked, so make sure paperwork is correct before you go. The reward is a landscape of exceptional variety and very few people.
t.uvs lake@50.3,92.9:
Salt water in a landlocked basin, with snow mountains behind it and a horizon that goes on and on: Uvs Lake is a strange, quiet sight. It sits low, at around seven hundred metres above sea level, in a basin on the Mongolia and Tuva border, and it has no outlet. Water arrives from the rivers, mainly the Tes, and leaves only by evaporation, which is why the lake is salty and why its shape changes from year to year.

The shoreline is a mixed mess of reeds, mudflats, sandbars and wet meadow, and that is where the interest lies. In May and June and again in September, the shallows are filled with migrating birds, including pelicans, swans, bar-headed geese and many waders. The surrounding steppe has a light smell of sage and dry grass, and when the wind drops you can hear birds from a long way off. Across the water the Altai and Tannu-Ola ranges stand blue in the distance.

The lake has a long record of local use. Herders bring their animals to the shore pastures in summer, and nomadic families still follow the old pattern of moving between seasonal camps. Burial mounds and standing stones scattered around the basin show that people have lived and travelled here since the Bronze Age, and the Scythian-era tombs of Tuva, not far north, are among the richest ever found.

Riding to the shore means tracks across steppe, with soft patches near the water that can bog a loaded bike. Stop well back from the mud, and do not try to ride on the salt crust after rain. Wind is a feature of every day. Go in late spring or early autumn for birds, summer for warmth, and always leave with a full tank.
t.beluga point@61.0,-149.7:
Turnagain Arm has the second-highest tides in North America, and Beluga Point is the best seat for watching them work. The Seward Highway runs along the cliffs here, squeezed between the Chugach Mountains and a long, silvery fjord that empties and refills twice a day with a tidal range of about nine metres. At low water you look down onto grey glacial mudflats; a few hours later the sea comes back, sometimes as a tidal bore, a single low wave that runs up the inlet at walking speed. The best views of the bore come an hour or two after low tide in Anchorage, and the locals keep a tide table the way others keep a weather forecast.

The belugas the point is named for are real, though they come and go. These small white whales chase salmon and hooligan, a smelt-like fish, into the Arm in summer, and on a rising tide you may see pale backs rolling in the grey water. Bring binoculars and some patience, and be glad of the pull-out, because the shoulder is a poor place to stop. Do not wander out onto the mudflats. The silt is fine as flour and sets like cement around your legs, and people have died when the tide returned before they could be freed.

The road itself is a beauty. The Seward Highway is an All-American Road, with two lanes, long passing sections, and corners that follow the water in easy curves, so it is relaxed riding rather than a technical test. Further along, at Windy Corner, Dall sheep often graze on the roadside slopes, which causes traffic jams of cheerful tourists. Speed enforcement is steady here, and the weather can swing from sunshine to rain and chill within an hour, with wind funnelled down the Arm. Layers matter, even in July. Late June and July give nearly endless daylight, and September brings gold on the birches and fewer people.

Beluga Point is about twenty-seven kilometres south of Anchorage, with no services at the pull-out. Anchorage, a city of three hundred thousand, has everything, and Girdwood, a little over twenty-seven kilometres in the other direction, has fuel, food and the Alyeska ski resort. Fill up before leaving the city, then take your time. Captain Cook, who sailed into the Arm in 1778 hoping for the Northwest Passage, found only a dead end and had to turn again, hence the name Turnagain.
t.glennallen@62.1,-145.6:
Alaska is big, and the Copper River Basin proves it. Glennallen sits in a broad, flat bowl of spruce forest and muskeg, ringed by some of the highest mountains in North America: the Wrangell Mountains stand to the east, with Mount Drum, Mount Sanford and the huge ice-clad bulk of Mount Wrangell, an active volcano that steams in cold weather. On a clear day the view from the highway is almost too large to take in, and a rider is aware of being a very small thing on a very long road.

The town itself is a service hub, little more than a crossroads where the Richardson Highway meets the Glenn Highway running to Anchorage. It was named after two army explorers, Captain Edwin Glenn and Captain Henry Allen, who surveyed the region in the 1890s, in a search for a route to the Klondike and to the interior. Gold, copper and later the Trans-Alaska Pipeline, whose silver pipe crosses the country beside the road, have all shaped the area. The Native people of the region, the Ahtna Athabaskans, have lived along the Copper River for thousands of years, and the river's red salmon run is central to their culture and to the local economy.

The riding is long, open and sometimes rough. The Richardson Highway, the oldest in Alaska, runs for hundreds of miles between Valdez and Fairbanks, and it is mostly paved and well maintained, but frost heaves can toss a bike off line, and gravel patches appear without warning. Mosquitoes are ferocious in June and July, so bring repellent, and weather can change in an hour from warm sunshine to cold rain. In summer, daylight lasts almost around the clock, which makes late starts possible.

Fuel is the thing to plan around. Glennallen has stations, food and lodging, and it is the largest settlement for a long way in any direction, so take fuel here whenever you pass. Distances between services north and south can be long, and a reserve can in practice be life-saving. The road to McCarthy, a gravel track into the Wrangell-St Elias National Park, starts at Chitina, a good way south-east.

Late May to early September is the usable season. Autumn comes early, and by mid-September the tundra turns red and gold, and snow can fall.
t.thompson pass@61.1,-145.7:
Thompson Pass sits at 855 metres, which sounds like nothing until you remember that the sea is only a few dozen kilometres behind you. The Chugach Mountains rise straight out of Prince William Sound, they catch every storm that comes in off the Gulf of Alaska, and this notch in the range is where the weather gets wrung out. The pass is famous for snow. It holds Alaska's records for snowfall, with a single winter in the early 1950s piling up close to a thousand inches, and the highway crews who keep it open will tell you stories you only half believe.

In summer the story is gentler but still wide open. Coming up from Valdez you leave the water behind and climb through Keystone Canyon, a narrow slot with waterfalls dropping off the walls right beside the tarmac, then the valley widens and the trees thin out. By the top you are above most of the spruce, in country of tundra, rock and snowfields, with peaks standing around in every direction. The Richardson Highway is a proper two-lane road, well surfaced, with long, easy gradients rather than anything tight, so this is a pass for looking rather than for hustling. Wind can be strong up here, and even in July it is worth having a layer in the tank bag, because the temperature drops several degrees between Valdez and the summit.

The road has a longer history than most Alaskan highways. It began as a pack trail in the gold rush years, a way for prospectors to reach the interior without going through Canada, and it was later improved into a wagon road and then a highway. It carries the name of an army officer who oversaw the early Alaska road commission. At the Valdez end, the Trans-Alaska Pipeline finishes its eight-hundred-mile run, and the oil terminal across the bay is the reason the road is maintained as well as it is.

There is nothing at the pass in the way of fuel, so plan around Valdez, a town of a few thousand people with everything a rider needs, and Glennallen on the other side. Pull in at the wide gravel turnouts and give the weather a minute to show you what it intends to do. On a clear evening the light on the snow is long and gold and the whole place goes quiet. On a bad day the cloud sits on the road like a lid, and the right decision is coffee in Valdez and a second try tomorrow.
t.worthington glacier@61.2,-145.7:
A few kilometres south of the top of Thompson Pass, the road swings round a bend and a river of ice is simply there, filling a side valley and hanging above a gravel bar. This is Worthington Glacier, and it is one of the few glaciers in Alaska you can reach on a motorcycle without anything more strenuous than putting the side stand down. There is a state recreation site with a parking area, a viewing platform and a short trail that leads up toward the terminus, close enough that you can see the blue colour in the crevasses.

The ice here comes down from a high icefield in the Chugach Mountains, and like most glaciers in the range it has been shrinking for decades. The trail has had to be adjusted over the years as the ice pulls back, and the meltwater leaves a landscape of fresh, raw gravel, silt and boulders. That raw look is the point. Plants have barely started to colonise it, and you can read the retreat as a series of steps in the ground. Cold air pours off the ice even on a warm day, so the walk up feels like opening a freezer door.

Riding to it from Valdez is a pleasure of the unhurried sort. The road climbs steadily out of the coastal rainforest and through Keystone Canyon before the mountains open up, and you reach the glacier a little before the summit of the pass. Traffic is light, and what there is tends to be camper vans and the occasional truck, so you can ride at your own speed and stop wherever the view demands it. Frost heaves are the hazard, as on every northern road, and they are usually marked with small flags or fresh paint. In wet weather the gravel in the parking area gets slick, so mind your footing and your boots.

Fuel is the thing to settle before you come. There is none at the glacier. Valdez, some thirty kilometres down the road and a town with a small harbour, a few cafes and the oil terminal's workers, is the place to fill the tank, and Glennallen is the next real stop to the north. Bring a warm layer and gloves even in summer, because the wind coming off the ice has a bite, and bring a camera that can cope with white on white. The best light is early or late, when the low sun picks out the ridges of the glacier and turns the meltwater lake the colour of milky jade.
t.tanggula pass@32.9,91.9:
Tanggula Pass is a place of thin air and big silence. At 5,231 metres on the Qinghai-Tibet Highway, it is one of the high points of the road that crosses the plateau from Golmud to Lhasa, and it marks the boundary between Qinghai and the Tibet Autonomous Region. There is little here but a stone marker, a wide view and a landscape of bare brown hills dusted with snow. You will feel the altitude as soon as you step off the bike: a pounding head, short breath and a strange slowness in your limbs.

The pass lies on the watershed between the rivers of the Yangtze to the north and the Salween to the south, and the glacier-fed streams nearby are the headwaters of the great Yangtze, which runs thousands of kilometres to the East China Sea. The plateau around it is a high, cold desert, home to wild yaks, Tibetan antelope and wild asses, and the horizon seems endless.

The railway runs alongside the road here, and the Tanggula station on the Qinghai-Tibet line, at over 5,000 metres, is among the highest in the world. Engineers had to deal with permafrost, using cooling pipes and raised tracks to keep the ground frozen, and the highway has a similar story of repair and renewal. The road itself is paved and generally in good condition, but trucks carrying freight up and down the plateau are heavy and slow.

Travel here needs planning. The altitude can cause serious sickness, and riders should acclimatise for days on the plateau before pushing over the pass. Foreign visitors need permits and typically a guide, and independent travel is restricted. Weather is severe, with snow possible in any month, strong winds, and temperatures that can drop far below freezing even in summer. Fuel is available in the towns on either side, such as Amdo and Nagqu, but not on the pass, and you should fill the tank in good time. Bring warm clothes, water and patience, and treat the stop as a short one.
t.nagqu@31.5,92.1:
Nagqu is the biggest town you will meet on the northern half of the Tibetan plateau, and it feels like a frontier. It sits at roughly 4,500 metres on the open grassland between the Tanggula range and Lhasa, a high, cold country of yak herders, black tents and wide rolling pasture, and the Chinese name for it is Naqu. The Tibetan name means the black river, and the pastures around it have fed nomadic families for centuries.

Every August the town holds a horse festival that draws herders from across the region, with races, archery, wrestling and a great deal of tea. The tents spread across the grassland, riders in colourful dress gallop past, and the whole scene is one of the liveliest in Tibet. Outside festival time Nagqu is a working place, a crossroads for trucks on the Qinghai-Tibet highway and the road east toward Sichuan, with straight streets, shops, noodle restaurants and a certain frontier toughness.

The highway through here is smooth and fast by plateau standards, but altitude changes everything. Engines lose power in thin air, a carburetted bike may run rich and cough, and riders themselves tire more quickly and think more slowly. Sleep at this height can be poor, headaches are common, and anyone arriving from low ground should take it easy. The weather is harsh: strong winds, hail and snow can arrive in any month, and temperatures swing hard between day and night.

There is plenty of fuel in town, as you would expect of a place of thirty thousand people on a major road, and it is the sensible place to top the tank before the long stretches on either side. Food is simple and filling, with yak meat, noodles and butter tea, and a warm room is welcome after a day in the wind. Lhasa lies a long day to the south, and the road in between drops gradually off the high grassland toward the valleys of central Tibet.

For foreign visitors, travel on this route requires permits and normally a guide, and the rules change, so confirm everything with an operator before you plan. The light in the early morning is wonderful, low and clear over a pale landscape, and a short walk before the traffic wakes up is a good way to meet the place.
t.pointe venus@-17.5,-149.5:
Pointe Venus is a low finger of black volcanic sand poking into the Pacific just north of Papeete, and it is the gentlest start you could ask for on a lap of Tahiti. The coast road, the RDO as locals call it, runs straight through Mahina, and a short side lane leads out past the casuarina trees to a car park by the beach. Arue and Pirae, the suburbs of the capital, are a few minutes behind you, so you arrive here still half in town traffic and with the whole island ahead.

The name is not a tourist invention. James Cook came ashore on this point in 1769 to watch Venus cross the face of the sun, a measurement that was supposed to help work out the distance between the earth and the sun. Nearby stands a memorial to that expedition, and the lighthouse on the point has been a navigation mark for ships feeling their way toward the reef passes for well over a century. A little further along, a monument recalls the arrival of the first Protestant missionaries in 1797, which shaped a great deal of island life afterwards, including the hymn singing you may hear drifting out of village churches on a Sunday.

For a rider the interest is mostly in what surrounds the stop. The sand is dark and hot underfoot, so boots are better than flip-flops if you want to walk to the lighthouse, and the water is shallow and calm enough on the sheltered side for a proper dip. Morning is best, before the trade wind picks up and before the day-trippers from the capital arrive. Light from the east lifts Moorea on the horizon in a way you will not see after lunch.

Practicalities are simple. Mahina is a real town with several thousand residents, so fuel, a bakery and a cold drink are all within a couple of kilometres, and you should top up here rather than gamble on the sparser stretches of the east and south coasts. The road surface along the north shore is good, the speed limit is low, and scooters and the island's brightly painted trucks, the famous le truck buses, share it with you without much hurry. Treat it as a warm-up lap, and keep an eye on the sky: afternoon showers can arrive suddenly, and the painted road markings go slick when they do.
t.tiarei waterfalls@-17.5,-149.3:
Past Mahina the coast road swings away from the lagoon and starts to feel like proper east Tahiti, with the mountains standing straight up on your right and a roar of surf on your left. Tiarei sits in that long strip of narrow plain, and the waterfalls above it are the reason to pull over. They are the Faarumai falls, reached by a short drive inland from the main road and then a walk through dense, wet forest of tree ferns, hibiscus and tall mape trees. The falls drop from the high ridges that hold the rain coming in from the sea, so the water is rarely absent, and in the wet months from November to April they thunder.

This side of the island gets far more rain than Papeete, and you feel it in the green. Everything drips, the moss is thick on the roadside walls and the air has a mineral, flowery smell, like a greenhouse with the door open. Riders who think of Tahiti as a beach with a road beside it are often surprised by how much of the circuit is rainforest, with heavy cloud sitting low over the valleys by early afternoon. If you want the falls looking their best and the path dry enough to walk without slipping, go in the morning and carry a light rain jacket anyway.

The coast road itself is a pleasure here, mostly flat with long gentle bends, a few one-lane bridges over rivers that tumble straight from the mountains, and dark volcanic beaches where surfers pick their way over the stones. Watch for loose gravel after storms and for dogs and chickens that regard the tarmac as a village square. Not far along the road there is also a blowhole at Arahoho where the swell pushes up through lava rock, which is worth a stop on a heavy sea.

Do not count on much here beyond a roadside snack stand or a small shop in Tiarei. Fuel is better taken in Mahina behind you, or at Taravao ahead, and it is wise to carry a little cash for the stalls. The access road to the falls can be closed after landslides, so if a sign says the path is shut, believe it.
t.teahupoo@-17.8,-149.3:
The road to Teahupoo ends rather than finishes. You run down the south side of Tahiti Iti, the small round peninsula hanging off the main island like a second thought, through villages with names that sound like a drumbeat, and at the end the tarmac simply gives up at a river mouth and a patch of grass. Beyond is the bush, a footpath and then the cliffs; nobody drives around the far side.

Out on the reef a few hundred metres offshore is the reason the whole world knows this tiny place. Teahupoo is one of the heaviest waves on earth, a thick lip of water that breaks over a shallow reef, and the name is often translated by locals with a grim joke about a wall of skulls. When a big south swell arrives, boats and jet skis crowd the channel and the road is lined with photographers. The Olympic surfing contest of 2024 was held here, and the tall judging tower on the reef became part of the skyline. On a flat day it is just a calm blue lagoon and a pass, and you can sit on the sea wall and wonder what the fuss is about.

The ride in has its own charm. From Taravao the road runs along the coast with the lagoon on one side and thick green slopes on the other, the bends easy, the surface decent but patched, and the traffic mostly local pickups and the occasional tour van. Watch for children and dogs in the villages, and for loose coral grit at junctions. The light is lovely late in the afternoon, when the ridge above the village turns gold and the air smells of frangipani, woodsmoke and salt.

Plan fuel before you come. Taravao, twelve kilometres or so back, is the sensible place to fill up, and there is little in the way of petrol out here. Small snack stands and a few guesthouses serve fresh fish with rice and coconut, and a lunch of poisson cru with a cold drink while you watch the lagoon is the correct way to end the road.
t.taravao@-17.7,-149.3:
Taravao is a neck of land, and you notice it the moment you arrive. Tahiti is two volcanoes joined by a narrow isthmus, a figure of eight lying on its side, and this is the waist. The coast road from Papeete splits here: one arm heads on around Tahiti Nui toward Teahupoo, the other climbs to the plateau and the viewpoint over the isthmus. For a rider it is the island's junction, supply point and breathing space all at once.

The town itself is practical rather than pretty. Afaahiti and Taravao have grown together into a community of several thousand, with supermarkets, petrol stations, pharmacies, a market and bakeries that open early. It is the one place on the south and east loop where you can confidently fill the tank, buy water and find a proper sandwich. Take advantage, because both Teahupoo and the long quiet shore to the west have little beyond small shops.

What makes Taravao worth more than a pit stop is the plateau above it. A road climbs into cooler air through pasture, with dairy cows grazing on green fields that look oddly like Normandy under tropical sky. Higher still the road gives views down the isthmus, with the sea on both sides, and on a clear morning you can see across the channel to Moorea. It is cooler, quieter and a good deal less hurried than the coast, and the bends are easy, though rain falls often and the tarmac can be greasy where trees overhang.

The place has a military past, since the French garrison built a fort here in the nineteenth century, and the isthmus has always been strategic as the only land link between the two halves of the island. Locals will tell you the area has a slightly different character from Papeete, more farming, more fishing and more slow Sunday lunches. If you arrive in the late morning, you might pick up fruit from a roadside stall, mangoes or pamplemousse the size of a child's head, and eat it sitting on the kerb.

The best time to come is early, when the light is soft and the supermarkets are empty. Then you can take the road onward with a full tank and some idea of what to expect.
t.girdwood@60.9,-149.2:
Girdwood is a ski town tucked into a valley of rainforest, and it seems an odd thing to find in Alaska until you see how much snow the Chugach Mountains collect. The town lies at the head of a green valley a few miles from the sea, with glaciers hanging from the peaks above and a hotel and chairlift complex, Alyeska, at the top of the road. Its streets wind between spruce and hemlock, and the air smells of rain, resin and cold water.

The town has had a hard history. The original settlement stood nearer the sea, on the flats of Turnagain Arm, until the great earthquake of 1964, which dropped the ground by several feet and let the tide flood the town. The old townsite was abandoned and the community rebuilt on higher ground, and the ghost forest of dead spruce, killed by salt water, can still be seen from the highway along the arm. The area was a gold-mining region in the early twentieth century, and an old mining creek, Crow Creek, still attracts visitors who like to pan for gold.

The ride here is among the best in Alaska. The Seward Highway runs along the shore of Turnagain Arm from Anchorage, a long, glorious road between the water and the mountains, with beluga whales sometimes visible from the roadside in summer and Dall sheep on the cliffs. The surface is mostly good, but the road is busy in summer, with tour buses, trucks and campers, and fast traffic with limited passing opportunities, so patience is wise. A strong wind often blows along the arm, and the tides here are among the biggest in North America, creating a bore tide that can be watched from the shore at certain times.

Girdwood has a modest set of services, with a petrol station, a few cafés and restaurants, a grocery store and several lodgings, so it is a good place to stop and fill the tank. Local food leans toward salmon, halibut and craft beer, and the restaurants serve hearty meals that suit cold weather. Rain is frequent, and temperatures even in summer can be cool, so carry a waterproof layer and warm gloves.

Take a short drive up to the ski resort if you have time. The tram climbs to a spot with a view over the glaciers, and the whole valley seems to open out below.
t.turnagain pass@60.8,-149.2:
Turnagain Pass is a low, wide opening in the Kenai Mountains, only about 1,000 feet above the sea, but it feels like the top of the world, since the peaks on either side hold snow most of the year. The Seward Highway crosses it between Girdwood and the Kenai Peninsula, running through open subalpine meadows, willow thickets and stands of mountain hemlock, and the air has a clean, cold, mossy smell. In winter the pass is a great white bowl, thick with snow, where skiers and snowmobilers gather, and in summer it is green and quiet.

The name has a lovely origin. When Captain James Cook sailed up this inlet in 1778, searching for a Northwest Passage, he followed one arm of the water until it ended in mudflats, and then had to turn again, and so gave the waterway the name Turnagain Arm. The pass takes its name from the arm. Cook's party had not found the passage they hoped for, but they gave the district a name that has lasted. The tides in the inlet are huge, and the arm remains one of the great sights of Alaska.

The ride over the pass is good, a smooth highway climbing in easy bends through wide valleys with big views. In summer, wildflowers cover the meadows, and moose browse in the willows, and in September the tundra turns red and gold. Traffic can be heavy, with tour buses, trucks and RVs, and the road is also a corridor for wildlife, so watch for moose, especially at dawn and dusk, when they step onto the road without warning. Weather can change swiftly, with fog, rain and wind, and snow can arrive early, so carry warm layers.

There are no services at the pass. A large turnout offers parking, toilets and trailheads, and in winter it is crowded with vehicles and snowmobile trailers, but nothing is sold. Girdwood, seventeen kilometres to the north, has fuel and food, and Seward and Cooper Landing on the Kenai side have more, so fill the tank before you climb. Mobile coverage can be patchy.

Stop at the turnout if the sky is clear, and look at the snowfields. The pass is quiet in a way that few places on a main highway ever are.
t.kenai lake@60.5,-149.8:
Kenai Lake is the colour of a glacier-fed swimming pool, and it takes a moment to believe it. The water is a pale, milky turquoise, tinted by finely ground rock called glacial flour that streams in from the glaciers high in the Kenai Mountains, and on a sunny day it glows. The lake is long and narrow, around twenty-four miles, curling between steep, snow-capped ridges, with spruce and birch forest along the shore and the sound of water moving everywhere.

The Seward Highway runs beside it for several miles, and this is one of the loveliest stretches of the road. The highway hugs the shore, then climbs a little to give a view down the lake to the mountains beyond, with pull-outs where you can stop and look. In summer the air smells of spruce and fresh water, and in September the cottonwoods and birches turn yellow. The Kenai River, famous for its salmon runs, leaves the lake at its western end, and in July sockeye salmon fill the river, drawing anglers from all over the world. Bears also come to fish, so be aware.

The road is a good one for riding, with smooth tarmac, easy bends and spectacular scenery, but it carries a lot of summer traffic, including RVs, fishing parties and tour vehicles, and speeds are modest. Wind can blow up the lake, and weather changes quickly, with rain common and snow possible in the high country early or late in the season.
